explain.summary: Water pulls heat out of Jonah's body many times faster than air at the same temperature, so a sunny day doesn't help him while he's in the lake. His body guards its core temperature two ways: muscles shiver to make heat, and blood is kept away from the skin so warm blood stays near his organs — that's why his lips and fingers look pale.
rules: Shivering starts once the water is colder than about 70°F, and grows as it gets colder.
The longer he stays in, the more he cools; leaner bodies cool faster.
Blood flow to the skin drops as he cools, keeping his core steady.
Wrapped in a towel, shivering halves every couple of minutes — faster in warmer air.

source.fact: Water conducts body heat away up to 26 times faster than air of the same temperature.
Shivering is muscles contracting and relaxing; this movement warms the body.
Normal body temperature is about 98.6°F, within a normal range of about 97–99°F.

choice.why: The real starting point differs with body size, how long you're in and how active you are; 70°F is a teaching value.

choice.what: Cooling builds up over minutes, halving the gap every 4 minutes
choice.why: Bodies cool gradually, not instantly; this shows 'the longer you stay, the colder you get'.

choice.what: Less blood to the skin is shown as a percentage
choice.why: Narrowing skin blood vessels in the cold is the body's heat-saving move; the exact amount isn't measured here.

choice.what: Core temperature is shown as steady
choice.why: In a short swim the body protects its core; dangerous cooling is outside this model.

choice.what: 'Heat loss in water vs. this air' scales the 26× figure by the temperature gaps
choice.why: The 26× comparison is for water and air at the same temperature; we stretch it in proportion to how much colder than the body each one is.

illustrative: Jonah's ten minutes, the 58°F lake, the 75°F air and his build are made up for a fictional story.
The 0–10 shivering scale is a teaching scale.

citations.title: The Hazards of Cold Water Boating
citations.supports: Water conducts body heat away up to 26 times faster than air of the same temperature; cold water quickly makes hands and feet numb.

citations.title: Chills
citations.supports: Shivering makes your muscles contract and relax; this involuntary movement warms your body, and can happen when you are exposed to low temperatures.

citations.title: Body temperature norms
citations.supports: Average normal body temperature is generally accepted as 98.6°F (37°C), with a normal range of about 97°F to 99°F.

does: Shows shivering starting once the water is cold enough and growing as it gets colder
Shows blood flow to the skin dropping so warm blood stays near the organs
Shows why warm air doesn't help much while you're in cold water
doesnt: Measure any real person — the numbers are illustrative teaching values
Show core temperature dropping; dangerous cold is outside the model
Include wind, swimming effort or wet clothes
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: If someone can't stop shivering or seems confused in the cold, get an adult right away.
